## Transforming Data in SQL: Counting Values `COUNT` {.scrollable}

- We can count the rows using `COUNT(*)`, which includes NULL and duplicate values

- We can count the values of a specific column using `COUNT(column_name01)` which includes duplicate values

- We can count the non-duplicate and non-NULL values of a specific column using `COUNT(DISTINCT column_name01)`

## How many people were booked into jail at two or more time points? {.scrollable}

`dbGetQuery(con,`\
`'SELECT jacket_number, COUNT(DISTINCT booking_number) AS total_bookings`\
`FROM ccso_jail01`\
`GROUP BY jacket_number`\
`HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT booking_number) > 1`\
`ORDER BY total_bookings DESC;')`

## String Manipulation in SQL {.scrollable}

- Useful string functions and operators that work in MySQL

| SQL | Description | Example | R or Tidyverse Analog |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `LENGTH(string01)` | returns the number of characters | `SELECT LENGTH(First_name) AS nchar FROM ccso_jail01` | `nchar()`; `str_count()` |
| `column_name01 LIKE "wildcard_syntax_pattern"` | returns 1 if string matches the pattern, 0 otherwise | `SELECT First_name LIKE "B%" FROM ccso_jail01` OR `SELECT First_name FROM ccso_jail01 WHERE First_name LIKE "B%" ORDER BY First_name` | `str_detect()` |
| `column_name01 REGEXP "regex_syntax_pattern"` | returns 1 if string matches the pattern, 0 otherwise | `SELECT First_name REGEXP "^[^AEIOU]" FROM ccso_jail01` OR `SELECT First_name FROM ccso_jail01 WHERE First_name REGEXP "^[^AEIOU]" ORDER BY First_name` | `str_detect()` |
| `CONCAT(string01, 'separator', string02)` | combines or concatenates strings together | `SELECT CONCAT(First_name, " ", Last_name) AS full_name FROM ccso_jail01` | `paste()`; `glue()` |
| `SUBSTRING(string01, starting_position, ending_position)` | extracts substring from string based on position | `SELECT SUBSTRING(First_name, 1, 1) AS first_initial FROM ccso_jail01` | `substring()` |
| `REPLACE(string01, string_to_be_replaced, string_replacement)` | replace string with another string | `SELECT REPLACE(First_name, First_name, Last_name) FROM ccso_jail01` | `gsub()` |
| `REGEXP_REPLACE(string01, "regex_syntax_pattern", "string_replacement")` | replaces all occurrences of the matched patterns with another string | `SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE(First_name, "[ABC]", "!") AS nchar FROM ccso_jail01` | `str_replace_all()` |
| `REGEXP_SUBSTR(string01, "regex_syntax_pattern)"` | extracts the first occurrence of a matched pattern | `SELECT REGEXP_SUBSTR(Last_name, "[A-Z]+\\-[A-Z]+") AS nchar FROM ccso_jail01` | `str_extract()` |
| `UPPER()` | enforces upper case on all letters | `toupper()`;`str_to_upper()` |  |
| `LOWER()` | enforces lower case on all letters | `tolower()`;`str_to_lower()` |  |
| `CASE WHEN THEN ELSE END` | change values based on specific cases | `SELECT Last_name, CASE WHEN Last_name LIKE "WILL%" THEN "WILL-FM" WHEN Last_name LIKE "JACK%" THEN "JACK-FM" ELSE Last_name END AS new_name FROM ccso_jail01 WHERE Last_name REGEXP "JACK+|WILL+"` | `case_when()` |

- Common regex syntax that works within REGEXP operators and functions (above):

|  |  |
|:---|:---|
| `.` | matches any single character |
| `*` | matches zero or more occurrences of the preceding character |
| `+` | matches one or more occurrences of the preceding character |
| `?` | matches zero or one occurrence of the preceding character |
| `^` | matches the start of a string |
| `$` | matches the end of a string |
| `\\` | escapes special characters to match them literally |
| `[abc]` | matches any single character in the brackets (a, b, or c) |
| `[^abc]` | matches any single character not in the brackets (not a, b, or c) |

## Handling Dates and Times in SQL {.scrollable}

- Dates and times must be written in the following formats:

  - DATE... YYYY-MM-DD\
  - DATETIME... YYYY-MM-DD HH:MI:SS\
  - TIMESTAMP... YYYY-MM-DD HH:MI:SS\
  - TIME... HHH:MI:SS

- These 4 types are understood in SQL:

  - DATE
  - DATETIME
  - TIMESTAMP
  - TIME

| Date Format Code | Meaning                      |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------|
| %M               | Full month name              |
| %m               | Month numbered (01-12)       |
| %W               | Full weekday name            |
| %d               | Day of the month (0-31)      |
| %j               | Day of the year (001-366)    |
| %Y               | 4-digit year                 |
| %y               | 2-digit year                 |
| %H               | Hours (00-23)                |
| %h               | Hours (01-12)                |
| %i               | Minute numbered (00-59)      |
| %s               | Seconds (00-59)              |
| %f               | Microseconds (000000-999999) |
| %p               | AM/PM                        |

- Common functions to properly handle dates and times in MySQL

| SQL | Description | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| CAST(date_value AS date_format) | converts a value of one type to another type | `SELECT CAST(CONCAT(str_to_date(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y")," ", booking_time) AS DATETIME) FROM ccso_jail01` |
| `STR_TO_DATE(string01, "%date %format %code")` | convert string to proper date format | `SELECT STR_TO_DATE(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y") FROM ccso_jail01` |
| `CURRENT_DATE()` | print current date | `SELECT CURRENT_DATE()` |
| `CURRENT_TIME()` | print current time | `SELECT CURRENT_TIME()` |
| `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` | print current timestamp | `SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` |
| `EXTRACT(interval FROM date_string01)` | returns string based on date string and one of the following interval types: SECOND, MINUTE, HOUR, DAY, MONTH, YEAR, MINUTE_SECOND, HOUR_SECOND, YEAR_MONTH | `SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM CAST(CONCAT(str_to_date(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y")," ", booking_time) AS DATETIME)) FROM ccso_jail01` |
| `DATEDIFF(newer_date_value, older_date_value)` | return difference in days between two dates | `SELECT DATEDIFF(str_to_date(released_date, "%m/%d/%Y"), str_to_date(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y")) FROM ccso_jail01` |
| `column_name01 BETWEEN lower_bound AND upper_bound` | common range between dates | `SELECT str_to_date(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y") AS bd FROM ccso_jail01 WHERE str_to_date(booking_date, "%m/%d/%Y") BETWEEN "2019-06-21" AND "2019-09-22"` |

## Subqueries in SQL {.scrollable}

- Query structure is the same for subqueries but enclosed in parentheses

`(SELECT column_name01, column_name02`\
`FROM table_name01`\
`WHERE row_condition01`\
`GROUP BY column_name01`\
`HAVING group_condition01`\
`ORDER BY column_name01`\
`LIMIT number_of_rows OFFSET number_of_rows_to_skip);`

- Some subqueries can be executed independently, which means they are **non-correlated**

- Some subqueries will be executed for row that might be included in the resulting set, which means they are **correlated**

- When using a subquery in the `FROM` clause, it requires an alias using `AS` because it represents a derived table

## How many people were booked into jail at two or more time points? {.scrollable}

`dbGetQuery(con,` `'SELECT jacket_number, COUNT(jacket_number) AS total_bookings`\
`FROM (SELECT DISTINCT jacket_number, booking_number`\
`FROM ccso_jail01) AS j2`\
`GROUP BY jacket_number`\
`HAVING COUNT(jacket_number) > 1`\
`ORDER BY total_bookings DESC;')`

## String Manipulation in SQL: Concatenating Strings via `CONCAT()` {.scrollable}

- We can paste strings together with `CONCAT(string01, "separator_value01", string02)` much like `paste()` in base R

  - each `string01` and `string02` can be a literal string or a column in the data table; for example, last_name and first_name in the ccso_jail data
  - `"separator_value01"` is any character for separating the strings; for example, ", " as comma separator between last_name and first_name

## String Manipulation in SQL: Collapsing Strings via `GROUP_CONCAT()` {.scrollable}

- We can collapse strings to a single string for each group with `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT column_name_with_multiple_strings ORDER BY column_name_if_string_order_matters separator "separator_value01")` much like `paste(..., collapse = "separator_value01")`

  - `GROUP_CONCAT()` is typically used when there is a `GROUP BY` in the query; for example, there may be multiple crimes for each jacket_number in the ccso_jail data

  - `DISTINCT` is optional and removes duplicate string values in the `column_name` prior to collapsing them; for example, one jacket_number may have the same crime at a single booking

  - `column_name_with_multiple_strings` is ideally a column that has the strings for which you want to collapse; for example, crime

  - `ORDER BY` is optional and sorts the strings to be collapsed; for example, we may want to alphabetize the crimes or order them by final answer code

  - `separator "separator_value"` is optional and sets the separator character between the strings for collapsing; if omitted, the separator defaults to comma;

## Transforming Data in SQL: Summarizing with Analytic Functions {.scrollable}

- We have performed queries including summarized or aggregate functions and the resulting set may be **summarized** in the sense that the resulting rows correspond to the groups set in the query

  - Several summary or aggregate functions exist in SQL, such as `SUM()`, `COUNT()`, `AVG()`, `MIN()`, `MAX()`

- Analytic functions utilize the notion of "data windows" and "frames" in SQL

- "Data windows" are the grouped rows which allow the data to be partitioned per group so that an analytic function can be applied

- To create a window for the purpose of summarizing, we use `SUMMARY_FUNCTION01(column_name01) OVER(PARITION BY column_name_containing_groups)` within the `SELECT` clause

  - `OVER()` allows the summary function to be applied over all rows because there is no specified window or group of rows; for example in the ccso_jail data, we could compute the average number of crimes across all values of jacket_number using `AVG(COUNT(crime)) OVER ()`

  - `PARTITION BY` is optional and sets the groups to be windowed for the summary function; for example in the ccso_jail data, we could compute the total days spent in jail among the bookings per jacket_number using `SUM(SUM(DATEDIFF(released_date, booking_date))) OVER(PARTITION BY jacket_number)`

  - `column_name_containing_groups` is a column that contains groups of rows; for example in the ccso_jail data, jacket_number column

## Transforming Data in SQL: Ranking with Analytic Functions {.scrollable}

- There are three different ranking analytic functions that behave differently regarding ties:

- `RANK()`... yields same ranking for ties and skips ranking numbers based on number of ties; e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4

- `DENSE_RANK()`... yields same ranking for ties and continues ranking numbers based on number of ties; e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3

- `ROW_NUMEBR()`... ranks based on row appearance and yields un-ordered ranking for ties; e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4

- To create a window for the purpose of ranking, we use `RANK() OVER(PARITION BY column_containing_groups ORDER BY column_to_be_ranked)` within the `SELECT` clause

  - `OVER(ORDER BY column_to_be_ranked)` allows the ranking to be applied over the column to be ranked; for example in the ccso_jail data, after computing the total booked crimes per jacket_number, we could rank the total booked crimes using `RANK() OVER(ORDER BY COUNT(crime) DESC)`

  - `PARTITION BY` is optional but appears before `ORDER BY` and sets the groups to be windowed for the ranking; for example in the ccso_jail data, we could compute the total days spent in jail per booking per jacket_number and rank them using `RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY jacket_number ORDER BY total_days_in_jail_per_booking DESC)`

## Transforming Data in SQL: Accumulating Sums, Lags, and Leads with Analytic Functions {.scrollable}

- Analytic functions utilize the notion of "data windows" and "frames" in SQL

- "Data windows" are the grouped rows which allow the data to be partitioned per group so that an analytic function can be applied

- "Frames" are the precise rows to include in the "data window"
